body: Standard campaign-level Target ROAS gives no control over individual bids, so on thin-demand days the algorithm can pay very high CPCs. Its example: an ecommerce advertiser on tROAS saw CPC spikes up to $25 on low-demand days; moving into a portfolio with a $9 max CPC put a guardrail on budget blowouts while leaving Smart Bidding room to pursue the ROAS goal. Portfolios also pool conversion data across campaigns with the same target (for example 700% ROAS across all non-brand campaigns), which speeds learning and lets budget shift to better performers. Do not put campaigns with different goals (clearance versus new arrivals) in one portfolio, or campaigns too low in volume to benefit. claim: Google Ads credits conversions to the click date, so the last 3 to 4 days always look weak; judge recent days with 'conversions (by conversion time)' columns.
body: By default, Google Ads attributes a conversion to the date of the ad click, not the date of the purchase. If someone clicks on the 1st and the 3rd and buys on the 7th, the sale is written back to the click dates. Most other platforms log it on the purchase date. The consequence: when you open the account, the trailing three to four days (often the trailing week) show low conversions and ROAS in every account, because clicks from those days have not yet had time to convert and be written back. Operators who do not know this react to a dip that is not real, change bids or budgets, and can start a genuine decline. The agency's fix is to add the 'by conversion time' versions of conversions, conversion value and ROAS as custom columns, which count conversions on the day they happened and give a usable read on the last few days. How to apply: before any diagnosis, switch to conversion-time columns or exclude the most recent days; check the account's typical conversion lag in the path or time-lag reports; and widen the date range to a period that holds enough conversions for the account's volume, rather than reacting to one day.

claim: In a Google Ads decline, apply targeted fixes before any rebuild; restructuring resets learning and can start a spiral of falling performance and bigger changes.
body: Every rebuild or major restructure in Google Ads triggers a learning reset, which lowers conversion rate while the system re-enters auctions. The agency describes a common spiral: performance drops, the buyer makes a big change, learning resets and performance drops further, prompting another big change. Its rule is to default to a fix, not a rebuild, and to move to a rebuild only when the available fixes cannot plausibly close the gap to historical performance. Within fixes, avoid the 'kitchen sink': if conversion rate fell and you change the offer, page design and ad copy at once, you may recover but never learn which change worked, and the next time you must throw everything at it again. Decide by severity: in a dire situation, apply many fixes together and accept that you will not know why; in a moderate dip, apply one or two high-impact fixes, give them time to read, then add more. Be honest about expected impact: a headline tweak will not rescue a business-level decline unless the headline change caused it. Final gate: do not touch the account until you can finish the sentence 'this campaign is underperforming because this metric dropped, driven by this sub-metric, caused by this trigger'.

claim: Treat CPC as near-vanity: CPA = CPC / conversion rate, so higher CPCs only matter when conversion rate does not rise with them.
body: When efficiency drops in Google Ads, the agency splits it with two formulas: CPA = CPC / conversion rate, and clicks = impressions x CTR. Causes of a bad CPC rise: quality score changes (add expected CTR, ad relevance and landing page experience as keyword columns and compare before and after the inflection date); a new competitor (compare auction insights before and after); or more aggressive bidding pushing into costlier auctions that do not pay back. Landing page experience is the slowest to fix: the agency has waited weeks to months for Google to re-crawl and re-score after site fixes. If clicks fall instead, check impression share lost to budget versus lost to rank: hitting the daily budget means budget is the limit; falling clicks and impressions without hitting budget point to bid and rank (quality score, competition, bidding). Conversion-rate drops: check tracking, then landing page changes (URL, price, redirects, merchandising, upsells), search-term mix, a learning reset, or an ended promotion or free-shipping change.

claim: Use a feeder structure: a Standard Shopping campaign at a very low target ROAS (around 50%) for cold reach plus a high-tROAS PMax (around 600%) converting warm traffic.
body: The agency describes a target-ROAS trap. A campaign trailing about 4.2x gets a 400% tROAS; it stabilizes; the buyer nudges the target up in steps until spend starts to pull back near 500% to 600%. ROAS on the same $1,000 a day now reads 5x or 6x and looks like great buying, but the higher target has narrowed the campaign to people already likely to buy, mostly warm and returning visitors, and new-customer acquisition has shrunk. One campaign, usually Standard Shopping, runs a very low target ROAS (as low as 50%, or 0.5x) and is allowed to reach everyone searching the relevant terms, including cold audiences. Big Flare separates them into different campaigns so each shows its own ROAS, gives brand a much higher target, gives non-brand a lower target because its sales are more incremental, and shifts budget toward non-brand if the account is over-weighted on brand. Blue Sense says owners of some of the largest Google agencies agree in private: PMax claims too much, with half or more of its conversions coming from repeat customers or warm shoppers it did not truly acquire. Standard Shopping shows too little, because the cold shopper it found later clicks a PMax retargeting ad and PMax gets the last click. Put together, PMax looks like the engine of growth while Shopping is doing the real new customer work. How to apply it: give each campaign a job. Run standard Shopping on a lower target, aimed at reaching new shoppers. Run PMax on a higher target ROAS to convert people who have already shown interest. Judge Shopping on new customer numbers and total store revenue, not on its own ROAS. Read PMax's high ROAS as the cost of closing warm demand, not as proof it should get more budget.

claim: Build PMax with one asset group per product type, each with its own listing group, at least 15 products per group and 3 to 20 groups in total; Blue Sense tests with 200 asset groups did worse.
body: An asset group holds the headlines, descriptions and images PMax uses on search, display, YouTube, Discover and Gmail. Its listing group is the set of feed products it shows in Shopping. The biggest PMax mistake is keeping the single default asset group. The next biggest is building several asset groups but forgetting to narrow each listing group, so every group still contains every product and the split does nothing. Segment for four reasons. Relevant creative: someone who browsed jeans gets retargeted with jeans images and copy, and cold placements show jeans to people shopping for jeans. Sharper audience signals. Sharper search themes. And reporting, so you can see that tops are beating jeans this season and move budget. Rules of thumb: one asset group per product type, such as chairs, tables, lighting and decor in furniture, or hand tools, power tools, fasteners and accessories in hardware. Narrow each listing group to match. Keep at least 15 products per group, and never put one hero product alone, since it may barely spend. Run at least 3 and at most about 20 groups. Early PMax tests with around 200 asset groups showed simpler builds always won.

claim: Common Google account mistakes: GA4 as the primary conversion (missing 10 to 15% of sales), one PMax asset group, broad match on maximise clicks, display on in search, no negatives, and auto-apply recommendations left on.
body: Six errors show up again and again in Blue Sense audits. One, importing GA4 events as the main purchase conversion. GA4 misses about 10 to 15% of the purchases, sometimes more, that the Google Ads tag on the site records, so bidding works off less data. Use the Google Ads conversion tag with enhanced conversions and auto tagging, and keep GA4 as secondary. Two, running a single asset group in Performance Max with every product in it. Three, using broad match keywords with maximise clicks or manual bids; broad match needs smart bidding to work. Four, leaving the display network on in search campaigns, which wastes budget on one of the weakest networks, especially for cold traffic. Five, missing negative keywords: no brand negatives on cold campaigns, and no general negatives on search. Six, leaving auto apply recommendations on, which lets Google change the account in ways that rarely serve you. How to apply it: check each of these in the first hour of any audit; most accounts have at least one.

claim: Consolidation beats segmentation: three Shopping campaigns with 50, 20 and 10 monthly conversions each learn alone, and merging them into one with 90 usually lifts ROAS.
body: Each campaign mostly learns from its own conversions. Google shares a little data across the account, but treat campaigns as separate. Say three Shopping campaigns hold the same products and differ only in bid strategy. One gets 50 conversions every 30 days, one 20 and one 10. The campaign with 10 sets bids for future searches from just ten buyers, which is far too little to model, so it performs poorly. In accounts built like this, ROAS usually falls as conversion volume falls, and the low volume is the cause. The fix is simple: remove the two smaller campaigns and move their products and budget into the biggest. One campaign with about 90 conversions a month has a much richer data set, prices auctions more accurately and usually earns a higher ROAS. Make one campaign the starting point and demand a solid reason for every extra campaign. If you must split for business reasons, a shared portfolio bid strategy can pool the learning.

claim: E-commerce brands should put about 80 to 90% of Google spend into Shopping, not search, because shoppers see image, price and five rivals before clicking; B2B stores are the exception.
body: A search ad gives the shopper a headline, a description few read and some extensions. Someone searching for a red dress in size medium for a wedding learns the ad matches, but not the price, the look or the other choices, so many clicks land on a page that is not what they wanted, and in visual categories like fashion that hurts conversion. A Shopping listing shows the product image, price, title, brand, any promotion or reviews, beside about five competitors. The shopper compares six options and picks one, so they arrive already sold on your listing. That is why Shopping beats search in nearly every e-commerce business until you fill the Shopping network, after which search adds extra volume. So aim for about 80 to 90% of e-commerce Google spend in Shopping and PMax Shopping placements. The exception is stores with a business buyer side. A salon owner buying lashes in bulk or a cafe buying tea for resale skips Shopping listings with retail prices, because they want bulk rates and supplier terms, and clicks search ads instead. For these B2B stores, search can outperform Shopping.

claim: Each variant, such as 50 g, 100 g and 500 g sizes, can be its own Shopping listing with its own title, image and description, so each can target a different set of searches while sharing one product page.
body: Depending on how your feed is set up, each variant of a product appears as a separate Shopping listing. That is an opening most stores miss. If a creatine powder comes in 50 g, 100 g and 500 g, each size can carry a different title, image and description, even though all three send shoppers to the same product page. Use that to cover more searches. Give one variant a title built around one group of converting keywords, another a title built around a second group, and so on. You reach different shoppers with the same product and widen the range of searches you show on, without new pages or new products. How to apply it: export your search terms, group the converting phrases into two or three themes for the product, and assign one theme to each variant's title in a supplementary feed. Watch impressions, CTR and conversions per variant over the following weeks, and roll the change out gradually so you do not reset learning across the campaign.

claim: Exclude your brand from PMax twice, with a brand list exclusion and with brand negative keywords, so one catches what the other misses; without it PMax is mostly a retargeting campaign.
body: If PMax can bid on your brand name, much of its spend goes to people already looking for you, and it reports a strong ROAS for sales you would have had anyway. Blue Sense ranks brand exclusion as the second most important PMax setting after the feed. There are now two ways to do it. One: in campaign settings, open brand exclusions, add your brand, let Google find the related brand terms, and apply that list. For about a year this was the only option. Two: Google has since added negative keywords to PMax, so you can add brand terms as negatives directly. Use both as backups for each other. If you miss a spelling or variant in the negatives, the brand list should catch it, and if the negatives stop working for some reason, the list still protects you. Then run brand search in its own campaign so you still own your brand results. Check the PMax search terms report now and then for brand terms leaking through.

body: When time is short, work on PMax in this order. One, the feed: titles, descriptions and images in Merchant Center, because for a store most PMax spend goes to Shopping and the feed decides which searches you show on and how good your listing looks. This assumes the campaign really is putting most spend into Shopping. Two, brand exclusions: without them PMax mostly retargets people already searching for you. Three, asset group and listing group structure, plus the quality of the assets. Weak headlines, images and descriptions make weak ads on every placement outside Shopping. Four, the bid strategy and its target. Five, audience signals and search themes, which matter little once a campaign has data. How to apply it: in an audit or a 90 day plan, do not move down the list until the item above it is sound. claim: In Blue Sense tests, doubling Performance Max spend over 30 days kept its ROAS near 5 but barely moved store revenue, while ramping standard Shopping dropped its ROAS to about 3 or 4 yet added more real revenue.
body: Platform ROAS can mislead when you scale. Blue Sense ran the same test on many accounts where Performance Max and standard Shopping both showed about a 5x ROAS. On one account they doubled PMax budget over 30 days; on another they ramped standard Shopping. Every time, the extra back end revenue in the store was clearly better from the Shopping ramp. The platform said the opposite: PMax still reported about 5x after scaling, while Shopping's ROAS fell to around 4 or 3. The reason is that PMax retargets heavily and takes credit for purchases that would have happened, so its ROAS holds up as it spends more on warm people. Standard Shopping reaches colder shoppers, and many of those later buy through a PMax retargeting click, which gets the credit. On large accounts spending 100,000 to 300,000 a month in PMax, they saw more budget stop showing up in store revenue at all. How to apply it: when you scale Google, judge each move on store revenue or new customer revenue in the weeks after, not on campaign ROAS. A falling ROAS on Shopping while total revenue rises is a good result.

topics: max conversions vs max conversion value
claim: In e-commerce, choose value based bidding about 90% of the time: maximise conversions chases the cheapest orders, such as a 40 t-shirt at a 20 CPA over a 200 jumper with better ROAS.
body: Maximise conversions and target CPA try to get the most orders at the lowest cost per order. In a store that pushes budget toward the cheapest, easiest products to sell. Take a 40 t-shirt and a 200 jumper. The shirt might cost about 20 per order to sell, giving a 2x ROAS. The jumper might cost about 60 per order but return about 3.5x. A conversions strategy does not care about value or ROAS, so it puts the money behind the shirt because each order is cheaper, even though the jumper makes more revenue per dollar spent. The same logic pulls spend away from high ticket and bundle products across the catalogue. So for e-commerce, use maximise conversion value or target ROAS in about 90% of cases. Keep conversion based bidding for cases where every order is worth roughly the same, or where you deliberately want first orders on a low priced entry product and you track what those customers are worth later.

fails_when: Single product or flat price stores, where every order has similar value, or entry offers built on proven repeat value.

claim: Maximise conversion value keeps exploring new searches and people, while target ROAS near actual ROAS explores almost nothing; rotate between them over long periods so the account does not narrow and decline.
body: Think of bid strategies as expansive or restrictive. Maximise conversions and maximise conversion value are expansive: they can enter any auction they think will produce results. Target CPA and target ROAS are restrictive: they skip auctions unless the efficiency target looks safe. An easy way to picture it is a testing share. Blue Sense describes an expansive campaign as if it spent something like 30% of budget trying new keywords, audiences, placements and regions that are adjacent to past buyers but unproven. That exploring is what finds new pockets of demand and lets you scale. A restrictive campaign has close to 0% for testing when the target is close to or above actual results, for example a 4.5 target on a campaign doing 4.0. If the gap is wide, say a 2.0 target on a campaign doing 5.0, it behaves more like the expansive version. The upside of restrictive is efficiency; the downside is that the audience stops evolving with the business and platform. Staying on a tight target for a very long time can trap the account. Blue Sense rotates between the two over extended periods.
conditions: Accounts with stable conversion data on smart bidding that want growth as well as efficiency.
fails_when: Strict budgets or efficiency floors where any period of looser bidding would break cash limits; then keep the target and widen it slightly instead.

claim: Most brands either overspend on Google because it claims credit for demand Meta created, or cap it far too low, like 10,000 a month beside 250,000 on Meta, in a category with plenty of cold search demand.
body: Google sits at the bottom of the funnel. Meta, TikTok and affiliates create much of the demand, then shoppers search and Google captures them and reports a high ROAS. Brands that trust that ROAS keep raising Google spend even though much of it is not adding new sales, so they overspend. The opposite group has learned this lesson too well. They treat Google as only a demand capture tool and refuse to scale it, for example holding Google at 10,000 a month while spending a quarter of a million a month on Meta. In many categories that is a mistake, because large numbers of new buyers search every day for terms the product could serve, and Google can reach them profitably. How to decide which camp you are in: look at how much of your Google spend and revenue is brand search, check new customer results rather than platform ROAS, and test whether more spend on non brand Shopping and search moves total business revenue. Then use keyword research to see how much non brand search demand exists for your category before deciding Google has no room to grow.

claim: On search campaigns, split test landing pages by running two copies of an ad to different pages for 30 to 60 days, keep the winner and test again; a store converting 2x better can pay 2x per click.
body: In the end Google is an auction, and whoever can afford to pay most for a click wins it. What you can afford depends on revenue per visitor, which is conversion rate times order value. If your site converts twice as well as a rival's, you can pay twice as much per click and earn the same, so you can outbid them on the terms that matter. A competitor with better conversion and order value can beat you even with worse ads and structure. All the account work, from segmentation to feeds, only improves which auctions you enter and your quality score. Few advertisers test the page itself. How to do it: in a search ad group, duplicate the ad and point the copy at a second landing page. Run both for 30 to 60 days and compare conversion rates. Keep the winner, switch the loser off, and bring in a third page to test against the winner. Repeat, and work on order value too. Each win lifts revenue per visitor and lets you bid higher and scale. Blue Sense sees this as one of the biggest search levers.
conditions: Search campaigns with enough clicks per ad group to read a conversion rate difference within 30 to 60 days.

claim: On search campaigns, turn on smart bidding exploration so target ROAS can test outside the target in 10 to 30% bands; and treat limited by budget as a hint, not proof of room to spend.
body: Search campaigns have a setting called smart bidding exploration. With it on, a target ROAS campaign may go 10%, 20% or 30% below its target in some auctions to try searches it would normally skip. It sits between a tight restrictive strategy and an open expansive one: you mostly hit target, but the campaign keeps learning and can find room to grow. It is not available on PMax or Shopping. Separately, do not read the limited by budget label as a rule. It means Google thinks the campaign could have entered more auctions with more money. In practice it appears almost everywhere. Blue Sense runs PMax campaigns spending 5,000 to 10,000 a day in a small Australian market that still say limited by budget. Use it as one signal, then test extra budget in small steps and check whether store revenue and new customers rise with spend before trusting it.

claim: PMax search themes and audience signals are hints, not targeting; they matter on a new launch, but after about 30 days of conversions they are worth 1% at best, so ignore audits that tweak them.
body: Audience signals are not like old Meta interest targeting. They give a new PMax campaign or asset group a direction while it has no conversions, so it does not waste budget testing random people. Search themes do the same with keywords. Neither guarantees PMax will bid on those people or terms. When you set them, use keywords that already convert in your search campaigns and audiences that match the asset group, such as people in market for denim for a jeans group. Do not invent them. The more segmented your asset groups, the sharper these hints can be. But Blue Sense, after running PMax on more than 250 accounts and consulting on about 400 more, finds they hardly matter in a mature campaign. Once a campaign has about 30 days of conversion data, Google relies on that and bypasses the signals; you could remove them without any effect. On campaigns spending 30,000 to 100,000 a month in PMax, tweaking themes or signals is worth about 1% at best. So spend effort on them for new accounts, products, categories and asset groups, and treat an audit that focuses on them for a mature account as noise.

claim: Performance Max suits accounts spending up to about 15,000 to 20,000 a month; above that, most mid to upper market stores should keep only 20 to 40% of Google Shopping spend in PMax and run the rest through standard Shopping.
body: PMax is a good tool for smaller accounts. Under roughly 15,000 to 20,000 a month it gets an account moving and scaling with little setup. But it hits a ceiling: past a point, more budget no longer brings matching store revenue, even if the platform says it does. When PMax stalls, buyers usually try one of two moves. They raise budget and wait, or they raise target ROAS hoping to run more efficiently and then afford more spend. Both push more money into warm and repeat buyers, so PMax ROAS can rise while it becomes, in effect, a retargeting campaign. Change the question from whether to run PMax to what share of spend it should get. For most mid to upper market e-commerce and retail brands, Blue Sense puts that share at about 20 to 40%, with most spend in standard Shopping, which is better at reaching new buyers. Lead generation businesses can read search wherever this says Shopping. To grow new customer acquisition on Google beyond the PMax ceiling, add standard Shopping to the structure rather than forcing more into PMax.

claim: Portfolio bid strategies let separate campaigns learn from one shared pool of conversions and let you cap cost per click, such as 10 a click in high-end furniture, on target ROAS.
body: Campaigns normally learn on their own data, which is why splitting an account weakens each piece. A portfolio bid strategy is built in the shared library at account level and then applied to several campaigns. Those campaigns then share their learning as one pool. That is useful when you need segmentation for business reasons, such as separate campaigns for margin bands or product types, but do not want each one starved of data. The second benefit is control. A portfolio target ROAS or maximise value strategy lets you set a maximum and a minimum cost per click. In a category like high-end furniture, some auctions can push bids to 20 or 30 a click for very high intent shoppers, which the store knows will never pay back. A portfolio strategy can hold the target ROAS and cap clicks at, say, 10. Search Ads 360 offers similar features, but that is for large enterprise advertisers. How to apply it: if you split campaigns for real commercial reasons, group them under one portfolio strategy, and add a CPC cap where the product's margin sets a clear ceiling on what a click is worth.

claim: Raise Google budgets in steps of about 20%, never double them or halve a target CPA overnight; cutting budgets fast, even by half, rarely hurts.
body: Google is steadier than Meta or TikTok and drives conversions more consistently, and it reacts badly to sharp changes. On Meta and TikTok budgets can rise much faster. On Google, Blue Sense has found that throwing budgets around nearly always goes badly. The long standing rule of increasing budgets by about 20% at a time holds here. Doubling budget overnight is a bad idea, and so is halving a target CPA in one move, because both push the campaign into conditions its data does not cover. Bid strategy targets should change slowly too. Going down is different. Bringing budgets down quickly, even halving a large budget, has generally caused little instability or loss in their accounts. How to apply it: plan scale ups as a series of steps of about 20%, give each a few days to settle, and watch conversion value and new customers. If you need to save cash fast, cutting is safe. If a short peak needs much more spend, think about a separate campaign rather than a huge jump on a core one.

claim: Raising target ROAS step by step, say from 400% to 500% on a steady 1,000 a day campaign, lifts reported ROAS by shrinking bids to warm buyers; the lower target was likely winning more new customers.
body: A higher target ROAS does not make a campaign better at selling; it makes it pickier. To hit a higher return, Google limits which auctions it enters, and the people it drops are the cold ones. Picture all searchers for your terms as a circle. The inner part is warm: past visitors, existing customers, people who saw your Meta ads. Targeting only that part can reach a 7x return. To spend more, the circle widens to colder people and efficiency falls. Raise the target and the circle shrinks back toward the warm core. Here is the common trap. A campaign at about 4.2x trailing ROAS is set to a 400% target. Budget cannot grow, so the buyer pushes the target to 425%, then 450%, until spend starts to pull back near 500%. ROAS on the same 1,000 a day climbs and it looks like great buying, but the campaign has stopped winning new customers. How to check: compare new customer ROAS or new customer revenue before and after target changes. If reported ROAS rises while new customers fall, lower the target.

fails_when: Campaigns whose job is retargeting or brand capture, or stores where profit on returning buyers is the real goal.

claim: Start on maximise conversion value to build data, then switch to target ROAS set a little under trailing ROAS, such as 400% against 420% to 430%; it steadies daily results but does not raise average return.

On maximise conversion value, results swing week to week because the campaign makes big bets that sometimes win and sometimes lose. On target ROAS those swings flatten out. Over the whole period, though, average performance ends up about the same. The real gain is reliability: steady revenue from the platform each day, which most owners want. When you switch, set the target a little below the campaign's trailing ROAS, for example 400% when it has been running at 420% to 430%, so the campaign can still hit it without throttling spend. Then avoid the next step most people take, which is nudging the target up for more efficiency. That squeezes the campaign toward warm buyers and can start a spiral of shrinking spend. claim: Watch for CPC resistance once search impression share passes about 30 to 50%: if a 10% budget rise brings a 15 to 20% CPC rise, stop vertical scaling and expand into new terms or channels.
body: Aaron Young describes two ways to grow Google spend. Vertical scaling means more budget into the same products, campaigns and keyword themes. Horizontal scaling means reaching new demand: feature-led search terms, new products, YouTube and colder audiences. He coined CPC resistance for the point where vertical scaling stops paying: you add 10% budget and cost per click rises 15 to 20%, so the extra money buys about the same sales at a higher price and margin disappears. A theme might scale from 1,000 to 20,000 and then hit this wall. The signal to watch is search impression share. Before 2024 he could push about 90% of accounts to roughly 65% impression share; now resistance shows up between about 30 and 50%, depending on keyword theme and auction. How to apply: after each budget step, compare the change in spend, CPC and conversions over matching periods. If CPC climbs faster than budget and conversions do not rise in line, you have hit the ceiling; hold that campaign and put new money into horizontal moves.

fails_when: CPCs rise because of a seasonal auction spike such as Black Friday or a new competitor, not your own budget; the 30 to 50% band varies a lot by keyword theme and market.

claim: When a budget-limited campaign beats its target ROAS by a wide margin (say 500% actual against a 300% target), remove the target and run Maximize Conversion Value instead.
body: Ahead of Google's 17 August bidding change, Aaron Young's team sorted budget-limited campaigns with a target ROAS into three cases. Case one: actual return far above target, such as a 300% target delivering 500%. They expected the update to pull results down towards the target, so they removed the target and switched to Maximize Conversion Value. Case two: actual return within about 10 to 20% of target, so roughly 250% to 350% against 300%. They left those alone, knowing results would drift towards 300%. Case three: their example was a 200% target delivering 300%; here they raised the budget until the limited by budget warning disappeared. Because they did this in advance, their accounts avoided big jumps. The wider lesson: a target set well below what a campaign actually earns lets Google spend down to the target, so a stale target becomes a ceiling on efficiency. How to apply: each month, compare each campaign's target ROAS with its actual 30-day ROAS, and check the bid strategy status for budget limits before changing either.

claim: A Performance Max campaign can drift from cold buyers to existing customers; check the search terms for brand and the audience report for customer skew, which points to a broken brand exclusion or a target ROAS set too high.
body: Each campaign type breaks in its own ways, so name the type before you fix anything. Performance Max can retarget and can place across many channels, and it decides by itself how much to spend on warm or cold people. A campaign built and labelled for new customers can slowly end up serving mostly to people who already know or buy from you. How to check: open the search terms report for the campaign and look for brand terms. Brand should already be excluded, but confirm it. Then open the audience report and see whether delivery has shifted toward existing customers or site visitors. If brand terms have crept in, the brand exclusion is broken. If the audience skews to warm people, the target ROAS is probably too high, which makes Google favour the easy, likely buyers. A useful second read is new customer ROAS from a third party tool or from Google's own new customer reporting: a PMax campaign with a high target ROAS often shows poor new customer ROAS, while the same campaign on a lower target does better on new buyers.

If you, a colleague or the founder changed bids, budgets, feeds or targets recently, that edit may be the cause, and starting an audit on top of fresh changes makes the result impossible to read. On shared accounts this matters even more because nobody remembers every tweak. Second, zoom out. Judging a campaign on one or two days means working off a very small sample, which leads to changes that should never have been made. Set the range to the last 90 to 180 days and switch the chart to weekly, then look for a real inflection point rather than daily noise. How long to zoom out depends on conversion volume: an account with few sales needs a longer window before any trend is real. claim: Break every Google result into its parts before acting: CPA is CPC divided by conversion rate, and clicks are impressions times click through rate; these two cover about 90% of diagnoses.
body: Every campaign number you care about is the product of two or three smaller numbers, and each smaller number has different causes. So find which part moved before you look for a fix. Attributed revenue in Google comes from cost per click, conversion rate and average order value. If conversions fell, either clicks fell, conversion rate fell or tracking broke. The two formulas to keep in mind are: cost per acquisition equals cost per click divided by conversion rate, and clicks equal impressions times click through rate. If efficiency fell but click volume held, dig into CPC and conversion rate. If efficiency held but volume fell, dig into impressions and CTR. Go deeper where it helps. Average order value is a blend of new customer and returning customer order values, each with its own spread, and each order is driven by units per transaction and average unit price. If new customer order value fell because units per order dropped, the root cause is whatever changed units per order, such as a removed bundle. The deeper you understand these formulas, the closer you get to the true cause rather than a symptom.
conditions: Any paid account with enough conversions to compare periods; most useful in accounts with stable tracking.
fails_when: Tracking itself is broken, since every derived metric is then wrong; fix measurement first.

claim: Default to the smallest fix, not a rebuild: rebuilding resets learning and can start a loop of falling results and bigger changes; apply one or a few fixes at a time so you know what worked.
body: On Google, a rebuild or restructure throws campaigns back into learning. If you respond to a drop with a big structural change, results usually fall further, which tempts another big change, and the account spirals down. So once you have the root cause, apply a fix aimed at it and leave enough time to see whether it worked before trying anything else. Then decide how many fixes to group. If conversion rate on the landing page is the cause, there are many possible fixes: offer, design, better match between ad and page. If you do nine things and it recovers, you will not know which one mattered, and next time you will have to throw everything at it again. So when the problem is mild, apply only a few changes and learn from them. When the situation is severe, it is fine to change many things at once and accept that you will not know why it worked. Only move to a rebuild when fixes have failed or cannot close the gap back to the old baseline.
conditions: Google accounts with smart bidding that depend on learned conversion data.
fails_when: The account structure itself is the root cause, such as heavy segmentation starving campaigns of data, where consolidating is the fix.

claim: Google Ads credits a purchase to the day of the ad click, not the day of the sale, so the last 3 to 4 days always look weak until you add a conversions by conversion time column.
body: By default Google books a conversion against the date of the click that led to it. A shopper who clicks on the 1st, clicks again on the 3rd and buys on the 7th shows up on the 1st or 3rd, not the 7th. So any recent window is missing sales that have not happened yet but will be credited backwards later. The result is the same in every account: a 30 day chart looks steady and then drops sharply over the last few days, and a new buyer reads that as a crisis. How to apply it: in the campaigns view, open Columns, then Conversions, and add the versions labelled by conversion time (conversions, conversion value and value per cost by conversion time). These place each sale on the day it happened, so they give a fair read of the last few days. Use them whenever you judge recent performance, and never start a diagnosis, cut a budget or change a target because of the last 3 or 4 days in the default columns. Compare the two views side by side to see how long your typical click to purchase lag is.
conditions: Any Google Ads account; the gap is larger for higher priced products with longer consideration.
fails_when: Brands where nearly every buyer purchases in the same session as the click, so the lag is small.

claim: If both impressions and clicks fall while you are not spending your full daily budget, the cause is your bid strength, not budget; add search lost impression share by budget and by rank to tell them apart.
body: When efficiency holds but volume falls, the cause is fewer clicks, and clicks come from impressions times CTR. Impressions are lost for two reasons: budget or rank. Lost to budget means you are spending the full daily budget and more money would buy more impressions; if a 100 a day campaign spends 100 every day, raise budget to grow. Lost to rank means your bids are not strong enough to enter or win enough auctions. Add both columns, search lost impression share (budget) and search lost impression share (rank), to the campaign view. If spend has stayed the same but impressions changed, CTR may have risen as visitor quality improved, which offsets the change. If clicks and impressions are both down and you are not capped by budget, it is almost certainly the bid. Bid strength comes from quality score, competition and how aggressive your bidding is, so go back to those checks. On a CTR fall, an audience shift is the usual cause; real ad fatigue is rare on Google, though stale seasonal copy, such as a summer sale message after summer, can lower CTR on search ads.

claim: If cost per click rises while conversion rate stays flat, check quality score parts (expected CTR, ad relevance, landing page experience), new competitors in auction insights, and whether a bid change pushed you into pricier auctions.
body: Cost per click alone says little. It can rise with no harm if conversion rate rises too, because CPA stays the same; pricier clicks can be better clicks. It only matters at the extremes or when CPC rises and conversion rate does not. Then check three causes. One, quality score: in the keywords view add the quality score column and its three parts, expected CTR, ad relevance and landing page experience, and see which got worse after the drop. Ad relevance is the easiest fix: make the ads match the terms they show on. Expected CTR mostly reflects your current CTR, so the ads need to earn more clicks. Landing page experience is the hardest, because it needs site work and Google rescans on an unknown cycle; the presenter has waited weeks to months for the score to recover after fixing the page. Two, competition: compare auction insights before and after the drop to spot a new or more aggressive rival. Three, premium auctions: a target ROAS or bid strategy change may have sent you into more expensive auctions. That is only bad if the dearer clicks are not converting better.

claim: On Google Shopping, a sudden CTR and ROAS fall on a product often means a competitor discounted it; one Blue Sense client used a price watching script to pull products the moment a rival cut 20 to 30%.
body: Shopping shows your listing next to five or so others with prices visible, so price is a big part of who gets the click. If a rival selling the same item drops price by 20%, shoppers searching that product click them instead, and your CTR and ROAS on that item fall for reasons that have nothing to do with your account. Blue Sense saw this with a large sunglasses wholesaler: each time product level results fell, the main competitor had put that product on sale in Shopping. Rather than match the discount and give away most of the gross margin, they built a script that watched the competitor's site prices in near real time. When the rival cut price, the script pulled the product from the campaign or lowered its priority, so no budget went to a listing that could not win profitably. When the rival's price went back up, the product could return. How to apply it: when a single product's CTR drops, check competitor prices for that product first. claim: Only change the account when you can say the full chain: this campaign fell because this metric dropped, driven by this sub-metric, triggered by this cause; and size each fix honestly against the gap.

You must be able to say which metric dropped, which smaller metric drove it, what made that smaller metric change, and so what the root cause is. If you cannot complete it, do not touch the account. Always start at the top. When someone flags that a campaign's ROAS is down, first check the business. If total results are up and the campaign is the fifth biggest spender with a 10% ROAS dip, it barely matters. Then check other channels: a brand search campaign rises and falls with Meta spend. Only then go down to the campaign type, the campaign and the metric. Once you have a cause, ask honestly how much each fix can move the result. claim: When Google conversion rate falls, check in order: tracking and conversion time, landing page changes, a change in audience or search terms, a learning phase reset, then offer changes such as an ended promo or new free shipping threshold.
body: Work through the likely causes from simplest to hardest. One, measurement: has tracking stopped firing, and are you judging recent days without the conversion time columns, which always makes them look bad? Two, the landing page, usually the biggest cause. Did the ads start pointing at a different URL? Did the page change, did the price move, is a redirect sending people elsewhere, were upsells or cross sells added, or did merchandising change? Three, the audience. The same page converts better for higher quality visitors and worse for weaker ones. Compare search terms before and after: are clicks now coming from terms that match the page less well? Did a bid strategy change point the campaign at a different group of people? Four, learning. A big structural change can push campaigns back into learning, and while learning they enter the wrong auctions and send poorer traffic. Five, the offer. Did a promotion end, a discount come off, or the free shipping threshold change? Any of these lowers conversion rate with no change in the ads at all. Only once one of these explains the drop should you change the campaign.

claim: Keep Google campaigns few: at most two on a $10k a month budget and three to five under $50k, split only by category, margin, new versus evergreen, or stock grade.
body: Google works like Meta here: each campaign split divides the conversion data its bidding learns from, so there must be a strong reason you could defend for every campaign. Blue Sense's limits: with a budget around $10k a month, no more than two campaigns; under $50k a month, about three to five at most. Even at $1M a month, fewer campaigns usually perform better unless a split serves a business goal. How to apply: list your campaigns and write the reason for each. Merge any that share margin, goal and stock grade.

claim: Use a dynamic feed rule that pulls a whole fashion product from Shopping when its best-selling size sells out; ad efficiency on that product can drop by about 50% once core sizes are gone.
body: In fashion, a few sizes do most of the selling. When those go out of stock, the product still looks live in your ads, but most shoppers who click cannot buy their size. Blue Sense says paid efficiency on that product falls sharply, roughly by half, and the same thing tanks Meta ads overnight when a winning ad's core sizes run out. On Google you can prevent it with a feed rule. Identify the highest sell-through size for each product (often a medium), and set a rule that removes the whole product, every size, from the feed as soon as that size hits zero. Bring it back when it restocks. On Meta, pause or swap ads featuring that product, which is why multi-product creative lasts longer. Blue Sense lists size curve management as the main Google lever for brands spending $75k to $200k a month.
